3.title: The Tongue and True Wisdom
3.overview:
Chapter 3 addresses two related themes that together constitute one of the deepest diagnostics of spiritual authenticity: the tongue and wisdom. The tongue is the small member that reveals the character of the whole person; wisdom from above is the quality of character that the gospel produces and that shows most clearly in the way a person speaks and relates. Together they give James’s answer to a question implicit throughout the letter: what does genuine, gospel-produced faith look like in the texture of daily life?

The first section (vv. 1–12) on the tongue is the most extended treatment of speech in the New Testament. James does not merely say “control your tongue”; he shows why it is so difficult and why it matters so much. The tongue is small but has enormous power: the bit in the horse’s mouth, the rudder of the ship, the spark that ignites a forest fire. Its power is disproportionate to its size — and its power for destruction is disproportionate to its power for good. “No human being can tame the tongue” (v. 8): this is not resignation but diagnosis. The tongue’s problem is not primarily a speech problem; it is a heart problem. The spring produces what the source supplies (v. 11), and the source of the tongue’s poison is the unreformed heart.

The second section (vv. 13–18) contrasts two kinds of wisdom: the wisdom from below — earthly, unspiritual, demonic, characterized by bitter jealousy and selfish ambition — and the wisdom from above, which is “first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere.” The harvest produced by each wisdom is diagnostic: earthly wisdom produces disorder and every vile practice; heavenly wisdom produces a harvest of righteousness, sown in peace by those who make peace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Not many should become teachers, since teachers are judged more strictly (v.1) — for we all stumble, and the man who does not stumble in speech is mature, able to bridle his whole body (v.2). Bits turn horses (v.3); a very small rudder steers a great ship against strong winds (v.4). So the tongue is small and boasts great things — and see how great a forest a small fire sets ablaze (v.5).

The tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness, staining the whole body, setting the entire course of life alight, and itself set on fire by hell (v.6). Every kind of creature has been tamed by mankind (v.7), but no human being can tame the tongue — a restless evil, full of deadly poison (v.8).

With it we bless our Lord and Father, and curse people made in God’s likeness (v.9); from one mouth come blessing and cursing, and it ought not to be so (v.10). Does a spring give both fresh and salt water (v.11)? Can a fig tree bear olives, or a salt pond yield fresh water (v.12)?
verseByVerse.theology:
Why James Says It Cannot Be Tamed

Verse 8 is absolute and should be taken at face value rather than softened into “it is difficult.” Humanity has broken horses, trained falcons and charmed snakes — the fourfold list in verse 7 is the categories of Genesis 1, and the dominion given to Adam has really been exercised. And the same creature cannot govern six inches of his own mouth.

James shuts that door deliberately. If the tongue could be tamed by effort, the sensible response would be effort, and this would be a self-improvement chapter. It is not. The answer, when it comes at verse 17, is not a technique for controlling speech but a wisdom from above — because the problem was never the mouth. Verses 11–12 make the same point from nature: you do not work on the water, you deal with the spring, and no tree has ever been talked into bearing fruit foreign to it.

Note also the hopeful detail hidden in verse 4. The rudder is small and decisive, and it is steered — it goes wherever the will of the pilot directs. A rudder was never meant to be tamed. It was meant to be handled by someone.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Too many in that congregation wanted to teach, which is understandable in a Jewish setting where the rabbi was the most honoured figure in the community and teaching was the recognised route to standing. And James does not exempt himself — we who teach, we all stumble, we bless and curse. He is inside every indictment he issues.

Now: Verse 2 makes a diagnostic claim of great practical value: speech is the reliable index of maturity. Not doctrine, zeal, attendance or even generosity, all of which can be produced by effort or temperament. Most of what we say is not decided; it arrives — which makes it the most honest evidence available about what is inside, and is why the Lord said the mouth speaks out of the abundance of the heart (Matt 12:34). And verse 9 makes contempt a theological offence rather than merely an unkind one: you cannot bless the original and curse the image. Note the scope — not our enemies or the wicked, but people, without qualification.

verseByVerse.quote: Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers.” It is a startling opening, and it tells us something about that congregation: too many of them wanted the job.

That is understandable in a Jewish setting, where the rabbi was the most honoured figure in the community and teaching was the recognised path to standing. In scattered congregations with no settled structure, the man who could hold a room had an obvious opportunity.

“For you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.” Note the pronoun. James does not exempt himself; he puts himself inside the warning, which is the only honest way to issue it.

“Greater strictness” is a real principle and it runs through Scripture: to whom much is given, much is required. A teacher handles other people’s souls with his words, and error from the front does damage that error in a private conversation does not.

And this is the hinge into the chapter. Why does a warning about teachers open a passage about the tongue? Because teaching is the one occupation conducted entirely with it. The teacher is the man whose whole work is speech, and therefore the man most exposed to the thing James is about to describe.

Be clear that this is not discouragement of the gift. The New Testament commands teaching and prizes it. What James discourages is the wanting — the drift toward a visible role for reasons that have more to do with standing than with service. Anyone who has ever been eager to be heard should let the verse do its work before dismissing it.

verseByVerse.quote: For we all stumble in many ways. And if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For we all stumble in many ways.” Again the pronoun includes the writer, and the verb is the ordinary word for tripping — not falling headlong, but catching your foot. It happens repeatedly, to everyone, and mostly without intention.

Then: “if anyone does not stumble in what he says, he is a perfect man, able also to bridle his whole body.”

“Perfect” is teleios again, the word from 1:4 — mature, complete, having arrived at its end. James is not describing sinlessness but full growth.

And he is making a diagnostic claim of great practical value: speech is the reliable index of maturity. Not doctrine, not zeal, not attendance, not even generosity — all of which can be produced by effort or temperament. The tongue is the last thing to come under control, so a man who has it in hand has everything else in hand.

The reason is that speech is largely involuntary. Most of what we say is not decided; it arrives. Which makes it the most honest evidence available about what is actually inside — and it is why the Lord said that out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks (Matt 12:34).

“Able also to bridle his whole body.” The bridle image is from 1:26, and it introduces the two pictures that follow. James is not saying the tongue is the worst part of a person. He is saying it is the controlling part — and that is the thought the next verses develop.

verseByVerse.quote: If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well. Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two illustrations, and they make the same point from opposite ends of ordinary experience.

“If we put bits into the mouths of horses so that they obey us, we guide their whole bodies as well.” A horse weighs half a ton and can kill a man. The bit is a few ounces of iron. And the disproportion is the whole argument: a small thing in the mouth turns the entire animal.

“Look at the ships also: though they are so large and are driven by strong winds, they are guided by a very small rudder wherever the will of the pilot directs.” Same disproportion, and now with an added factor — the ship is not merely large, it is under enormous external pressure. Gales are pushing it. And still a board at the stern decides where it goes.

Both images say the same thing about the tongue: small, and decisive. James has already said the man who controls his speech controls everything (v.2); these pictures explain why. The tongue is not one member among many. It is the helm.

And notice a detail in the second: “wherever the will of the pilot directs.” The rudder is small and powerful, and it is also steered. It does not choose the course; somebody’s intention is behind it.

Which is the hopeful note in a chapter that is about to turn very dark. If the tongue is a rudder, the question is who has hold of it. James will say shortly that no human being can tame it — but a rudder was never meant to be tamed. It was meant to be steered.

verseByVerse.quote: So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things. How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire! And the tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness. The tongue is set among our members, staining the whole body, setting on fire the entire course of life, and set on fire by hell.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“So also the tongue is a small member, yet it boasts of great things.” The summary of the two pictures — and then the image changes, and the temperature with it.

“How great a forest is set ablaze by such a small fire!” The bit and the rudder were neutral instruments; a fire is not. James has moved from the tongue’s power to its danger, and every image from here is destructive.

Anyone who has lived near dry country knows the picture exactly. A cigarette end, a spark, one carelessly dropped thing — and a hillside is gone. The disproportion is the same as before, but now it runs the wrong way.

Then verse 6, and it is one of the most ferocious sentences in the New Testament. “The tongue is a fire, a world of unrighteousness.” A whole universe of wrong contained in one organ.

“Staining the whole body” — the word means to defile, to spot. “Setting on fire the entire course of life” — literally the wheel of birth, the whole revolving round of a person’s existence, alight from end to end.

And then the source: “and set on fire by hell.” The word is Gehenna — the valley outside Jerusalem where refuse burned continually, and the Lord’s own word for final judgement. James is not being poetic. He is saying that destructive speech has a supply line, and it runs from below.

This is the strongest thing said about the tongue anywhere in Scripture, and ask why James goes so far. The answer is in his congregation: these were people under pressure, poor, displaced, and quarrelling — and what was actually destroying them was not persecution from outside but what they were saying to each other.

verseByVerse.quote: For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind, but no human being can tame the tongue. It is a restless evil, full of deadly poison.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“For every kind of beast and bird, of reptile and sea creature, can be tamed and has been tamed by mankind.” The fourfold list is the categories of Genesis 1, and it is deliberate: the dominion given to Adam has actually been exercised. Humanity has broken horses, trained falcons, charmed snakes and worked with dolphins.

“But no human being can tame the tongue.” And there is the sentence the whole chapter has been building toward. Man rules the animal creation and cannot rule six inches of his own mouth.

The claim is absolute, and it needs to be taken at face value rather than softened into “it is difficult.” James says it cannot be done. Not by resolve, not by technique, not by the accumulated wisdom of a long life.

“It is a restless evil” — the same word he used of the double-minded man’s instability in 1:8. It will not settle; it cannot be left unattended.

“Full of deadly poison.” The image is the snake, and it is the one creature in the list that is not tamed but neutralised. The venom is not occasional; the tongue is described as full of it.

Now, why does James make a claim so absolute that it appears to leave no way forward? Because he is not writing a self-improvement chapter. If the tongue could be tamed by effort, the sensible response would be effort. He shuts that door deliberately — and the chapter’s answer, when it comes at verse 17, is not a technique for controlling speech but a wisdom from above. The problem is not the mouth. It never was.

verseByVerse.quote: With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God. From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“With it we bless our Lord and Father, and with it we curse people who are made in the likeness of God.”

This is the double-mindedness of 1:8 in its most visible form — and note the pronoun once more: we. James includes himself in the indictment.

The blessing is genuine. These are people who really do praise God — the same mouth was singing an hour ago. That is what makes the charge land: he is not describing hypocrites who despise God, but worshippers.

And the argument turns on a single phrase: we curse people “who are made in the likeness of God.” James reaches back to Genesis 1:26 and thereby makes cursing a person a theological offence rather than merely an unkind one.

You cannot bless the original and curse the image. The two acts are directed at the same likeness, and one of them must be insincere. It is the argument of 1 John 4:20 in different terms, and it is why contempt for people is never a small matter: the resemblance is still there in the man you are dismissing, however defaced.

Note also the scope. James does not say we curse our enemies, or the wicked. He says people — and the image-bearing is stated without qualification. It covers the difficult neighbour, the political opponent, and the person in the congregation who has genuinely wronged you.

“From the same mouth come blessing and cursing. My brothers, these things ought not to be so.” It is a remarkably restrained conclusion after the fire of verse 6 — almost gentle, and addressed to brothers. James thunders about the tongue in the abstract and speaks softly to the people who have one.

verseByVerse.quote: Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water? Can a fig tree, my brothers, bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs? Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three questions from nature, and each expects the answer no.

“Does a spring pour forth from the same opening both fresh and salt water?” The picture is local and vivid: around the Dead Sea and the Jordan valley there are both sweet springs and brackish ones, and no one confuses them. A spring is defined by what comes out of it, and what comes out is determined by what it draws from.

“Can a fig tree bear olives, or a grapevine produce figs?” Same logic in the vegetable world, and the Lord had made the identical point: you will know them by their fruits, since grapes are not gathered from thornbushes (Matt 7:16–20).

What all three have in common is that the output reveals the source, and that no tree or spring has ever been talked into producing something foreign to it. Which is the answer to a question the previous verses raise: if no human can tame the tongue, what is to be done?

The answer implied here is that you do not work on the water. You deal with the spring. Speech is a symptom, and the persistent attempt to reform it directly — watching your words, resolving to be kinder — is treating an outflow as though it were the problem.

“Neither can a salt pond yield fresh water.” The final line is blunt and it closes off the sentimental reading. There is no arrangement by which a bitter source produces sweet water occasionally. The two-mouthed spring of verse 11 is not merely inconsistent; James is saying it is impossible, and therefore that the blessing and cursing coming from one congregation is evidence of something wrong at the source.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show his works by good conduct, in the meekness of wisdom (v.13). But if there is bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and lie against the truth (v.14). That is not the wisdom from above but earthly, unspiritual, demonic (v.15) — for where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is disorder and every vile practice (v.16).

But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere (v.17). And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace (v.18).
verseByVerse.theology:
Wisdom Shown, Not Stated

The test in verse 13 is not an examination or a doctrinal statement but a life: “by his good conduct let him show his works.” Biblical wisdom is never primarily information — the Hebrew word is used of craftsmen who work metal and cloth — so the evidence for it is necessarily conduct rather than argument. A man may explain wisdom faultlessly and have none. It is the letter’s method applied to a new subject: faith is shown by works (2:18), wisdom is shown by works, and in both cases the demand is show me.

The order of verse 17 is deliberate. First pure means first in priority, not merely first in the list — which forbids the false peace that keeps quiet about sin to avoid trouble. Having secured that, peace governs everything after it. And notice what is absent from the whole list: not one quality is intellectual. Heavenly wisdom is described almost entirely in terms of how a person treats other people.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The two words in verse 14 name what was actually happening. Zelos is zeal, which can be a virtue, and is qualified as bitter — passion for a cause curdled into passion against a person. Eritheia comes from the world of hired political canvassing: working a crowd for your own advancement. And note where James locates them, in your hearts — the spring of verse 11. The quarrelling tongues had a source, and he has found it.

Now: “The meekness of wisdom” is the sting in verse 13. Prautes is not timidity but strength under control — the word used of a broken horse, all the power still there and now answering the rein. So the mark of the genuinely wise is that he is not pushing: he does not need to win the room, correct everyone present, or be recognised as the wisest person in it. In a congregation where too many wanted to teach, the eagerness to be seen as wise was itself evidence against the claim. And “open to reason” in verse 17 is an extraordinary thing to require of wisdom — willing to be persuaded — and exactly what the quarrelling teachers lacked.

verseByVerse.quote: Who is wise and understanding among you? By his good conduct let him show his works in the meekness of wisdom.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Who is wise and understanding among you?” The question returns to verse 1 and the men who wanted to teach. Very well — here is how the claim is tested.

And the test is not what you would expect. Not an examination, not a doctrinal statement, not fluency. “By his good conduct let him show his works.”

Wisdom in the Bible is never primarily information. It is skill in living — the Hebrew word is used of craftsmen who work metal and cloth — and so the evidence for it is necessarily a life rather than an argument. A man may be able to explain wisdom faultlessly and not have any.

This is the whole letter’s method applied to a new subject. Faith is shown by works (2:18); wisdom is shown by works; and in both cases the demand is the same — show me.

“In the meekness of wisdom.” The phrase is the sting. Prautes is not timidity but strength under control — the word used of a broken horse, all the power still there and now answering the rein.

So the mark of the genuinely wise man is that he is not pushing. He does not need to win the room, correct everyone present, or be recognised as the wisest person in it. And that is precisely diagnostic in a congregation where too many wanted to teach: the eagerness to be seen as wise is itself evidence against the claim.

verseByVerse.quote: But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts, do not boast and be false to the truth. This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your hearts.” Two words, and they name what was actually happening.

“Jealousy” is zelos — zeal, which can be a virtue and here is qualified as bitter. It is the passion for a cause that has curdled into passion against a person. And “selfish ambition” is eritheia, the word from the world of hired political canvassing — working a crowd for your own advancement.

Note where they are located: in your hearts. This is the spring of verse 11. The quarrelling tongues have a source, and James has found it.

“Do not boast and be false to the truth.” That is, do not claim to be wise while this is going on inside you. The claim is not merely mistaken; it is a lie told about reality.

Then the verdict, in three descending words: “This is not the wisdom that comes down from above, but is earthly, unspiritual, demonic.”

Earthly — it belongs to this world and reaches no higher. Unspiritual is literally soulish, natural, the merely human faculties operating without the Spirit. And demonic — which is where the descent ends, and it connects to verse 6: the tongue set on fire by hell, and the wisdom behind it coming from the same place.

“For where jealousy and selfish ambition exist, there will be disorder and every vile practice.” The word for disorder means instability, upheaval — the same family as the restless tongue of verse 8 and the unstable man of 1:8. And the sequence is worth noting: the private ambition produces public chaos, and the chaos then makes room for everything else.

verseByVerse.quote: But the wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere. And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the alternative, and it is the answer to the whole chapter. Not a technique for controlling the tongue — James has said that cannot be done — but a wisdom that comes from somewhere else.

“The wisdom from above” — the same direction as every good gift in 1:17, and the same thing offered to anyone who asks in 1:5. It is not achieved. It is given.

“Is first pure.” The order is deliberate; first means first in priority, not merely first in the list. Purity is not negotiable, and it comes before peaceableness — which forbids the false peace that keeps quiet about sin to avoid trouble.

“Then peaceable” — and having secured the order, James lets peace govern everything after it. Gentle is epieikes, the untranslatable word for the man who does not insist on the last inch of his rights. Open to reason means willing to be persuaded — an extraordinary thing to require of wisdom, and exactly what the quarrelling teachers lacked.

“Full of mercy and good fruits” — and there is the works test again. “Impartial” reaches back to chapter 2 and the gold ring. And “sincere” is anypokritos, without a mask — the opposite of the double-mindedness that has run through the whole letter.

Read the list and notice what is absent. Not one of these qualities is intellectual. Heavenly wisdom is described almost entirely in terms of how a person treats other people, which is what you would expect from a writer who has just said that wisdom is shown by conduct.

“And a harvest of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” The metaphor closes the chapter that opened with fire. Fire destroys in an afternoon; sowing produces slowly and only in the right conditions. And the peacemakers are not merely those who avoid conflict but those who make peace — which is work, and which is what the whole congregation had stopped doing.

4.title: Submit to God: Pride, the World, and the Brevity of Life
4.overview:
Chapter 4 is James’s most searching diagnosis of the spiritual condition underlying the community failures he has been describing. He has addressed partiality, dead faith, and the tongue; now he goes deeper to the root: the proud, self-assertive, world-oriented heart from which all these failures spring. The chapter has a single, sustained argument: the quarrels and conflicts that are tearing the community apart arise from desires at war within the self; those desires arise from the friendship with the world that the community has been cultivating; that friendship is adultery against God; the remedy is humble submission to God and resistance to the devil, which brings God near.

The chapter’s theological centre is the quotation from Scripture in verse 6: “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.” This verse (from Prov 3:34) is cited also by Peter (1 Pet 5:5) and was evidently a cherished early church text. It captures the fundamental dynamic of the human relationship to God: pride puts a person in the position of opposing God; humility puts a person in the position of receiving from God. All of the chapter’s practical instructions flow from this axis: submit, resist, draw near, grieve, humble yourself — all are the postures of humility before God.

The chapter ends with a brief but penetrating section on the presumption of making plans without reference to God (vv. 13–17). The language of the merchant who plans his itinerary without saying “if the Lord wills” is not a call to fatalism but to the contingency-consciousness that genuine faith produces. Life is a mist; tomorrow is not ours. The humble person holds plans loosely, not because planning is wrong, but because the presumption that the future belongs to us is always an act of practical atheism.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–10 — Quarrels, Adultery, and More Grace
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
What causes the fighting? Passions at war within you (v.1). You desire and do not have, so you murder; you covet and cannot obtain, so you quarrel — and you do not have because you do not ask (v.2). You ask and do not receive because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions (v.3).

Adulterous people! Friendship with the world is enmity with God, and whoever wishes to be the world’s friend makes himself God’s enemy (v.4). Does Scripture say to no purpose that he yearns jealously over the spirit he made to dwell in us (v.5)? But he gives more grace — God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble (v.6).

So: submit to God, resist the devil and he will flee (v.7); draw near to God and he will draw near to you; cleanse your hands and purify your hearts, you double-minded (v.8). Be wretched, mourn and weep; let laughter turn to mourning (v.9). Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you (v.10).
verseByVerse.theology:
But He Gives More Grace

Verse 6 is the turning point of the chapter and arguably of the letter. After the severity of verses 1–5 — quarrelling, coveting, misdirected prayer, spiritual adultery — four words open a door: but he gives more grace. More than the adultery, more than the appetite that has been running the whole congregation. Whatever the sin has cost, the supply is larger.

And the quotation from Proverbs 3:34 names the one condition. Grace is not scarce, but it is given downhill and will not flow to a man who has arranged himself above it. The word for opposes is military — to set oneself in array against. God does not merely withhold from the proud; he lines up against them. The ten imperatives that follow are simply the unpacking of the last word of the verse: the humble.

Note also the order in verse 7. Submit first, then resist — a man who has not submitted to God has no standing from which to resist anything. And the promise is that the devil will flee: he has no resources for a siege.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 4’s “adulterous people” is feminine in Greek — literally adulteresses — which is not an insult about women but the language of the prophets, where Israel is the bride and idolatry is infidelity. That reframes the whole chapter: the quarrelling and coveting are not merely bad behaviour but a marriage being broken. And divine jealousy in verse 5 is not the petty thing the English word suggests. A God who felt nothing about our adultery would not be more loving but less; indifference is not the opposite of jealousy, it is the opposite of love.

Now: Verse 1 makes an observation we rarely apply to church conflict. We look for the issue and the opposing sides; James says the war is within each person and the fighting outside is that inner war showing. Settle the presenting question and a man at war inside himself will find another. And verse 3 explains a great deal of unanswered prayer: these people are praying, but prayer has become the means of funding the appetites tearing them apart, and God mercifully declines. A father who financed every appetite his children presented would not be generous but negligent.

verseByVerse.quote: What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you? Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you? You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel. You do not have, because you do not ask.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“What causes quarrels and what causes fights among you?” The question is diagnostic, and James asks it the way a doctor asks where the pain is. Chapter 3 traced the quarrelling tongues to jealousy and selfish ambition in the heart; now he goes deeper still.

“Is it not this, that your passions are at war within you?” The word is hedonai — pleasures, from which we get hedonism. And note the location: the war is not between the factions in the congregation. It is within each person, and the fighting outside is that inner war showing.

That is the observation the chapter turns on, and pause over, because it is not how we usually analyse a church quarrel. We look for the issue and the opposing sides. James says the issue is downstream. A man at war inside himself will find something to fight about outside, and if you settle the presenting question he will find another one.

Then verse 2, and it is brutally compressed: “You desire and do not have, so you murder. You covet and cannot obtain, so you fight and quarrel.”

“Murder” is startling and has troubled readers. Some have proposed an emendation to “envy”, but the manuscripts do not support it. More likely James is doing what his brother did in the Sermon on the Mount — tracing the sin back to its root, where hatred is already murder (Matt 5:21–22; cf. 1 John 3:15). He is not accusing them of homicide. He is naming what the desire is on its way to.

Note the pattern repeated twice: desire → frustration → violence. The violence is not the primary problem; it is what unmet desire does when it is thwarted. And the frustration is essential to the mechanism — these people are not getting what they want, which is precisely why the room is on fire.

Then the diagnosis lands: “You do not have, because you do not ask.” After all that heat, the simplest possible sentence. They have organised their whole inner life around getting, and it has not occurred to them to ask the God who gives generously to all without reproach (1:5).

verseByVerse.quote: You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly, to spend it on your passions.
verseByVerse.commentary:
James anticipates the protest immediately. Somebody will say: but I have asked. And he answers it without softening.

“You ask and do not receive, because you ask wrongly.” So the problem is not that God is deaf, and not that prayer does not work. The petition itself is defective — and the defect is named exactly.

“To spend it on your passions.” The verb means to squander, and it is the word used of the prodigal son wasting his inheritance. The same word for pleasures as verse 1.

Here is the thing to see. These people are praying. They have not abandoned the practice; they have converted it. Prayer has become the means by which they hope to fund the very appetites that are tearing the congregation apart — and God, mercifully, declines.

That last word matters. An unanswered prayer of this kind is not God’s indifference; it is his kindness. A father who financed every appetite his children presented to him would not be generous, he would be negligent. James has already said God gives without reproach (1:5); he now says God does not give this.

And the verse quietly explains something that troubles many Christians. When a prayer has gone unanswered for years, the honest question is not only “why is God silent?” but “what would I do with it if I got it?” James does not apply that question to genuine need — he has just told them to ask — but he insists it be asked of desire.

verseByVerse.quote: You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God? Therefore whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“You adulterous people!” The Greek is feminine — literally adulteresses — and that is not an insult about women. It is the language of the prophets, where Israel is the bride and idolatry is infidelity. Hosea, Jeremiah and Ezekiel all speak this way, and James is invoking the whole tradition in one word.

Which reframes everything in the chapter. The quarrelling, the coveting, the misdirected prayers — these are not merely bad behaviour. They are a marriage being broken.

“Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God?” The word for friendship carries the sense of shared outlook — agreement, alliance, having the same tastes. And “the world” here is not the planet or the people in it, but the whole system organised without reference to God.

The claim is deliberately stark, and there is no middle category offered. James does not say friendship with the world leads to enmity, or risks it. He says it is enmity, and then repeats the point in the second half of the verse so that nobody can miss it.

“Whoever wishes to be a friend of the world.” Note the verb. It is not about being caught, or living in the world, or enjoying good things — the God of this letter gives every good gift (1:17) and richly provides. It is about where the affections are pointed. The wishing is the adultery.

“Makes himself an enemy of God.” The reflexive is important. God has not declared war on him. He has taken up a position, and the enmity is his own construction — which is exactly why the next verses can offer him grace rather than sentence.

verseByVerse.quote: Or do you suppose it is to no purpose that the Scripture says, “He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us”? But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, “God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 5 is the hardest sentence in the letter to translate, and honesty is better than confidence here. “He yearns jealously over the spirit that he has made to dwell in us” is one rendering; another makes the human spirit the subject, yearning enviously. And no Old Testament text says either in these words — James appears to be summarising a theme rather than quoting a verse.

The reading in the text is much the better one, and it fits the adultery of verse 4 exactly. God yearns jealously over the spirit he put in us. He is not indifferent to our infidelity; he wants us back, and wants us wholly.

Divine jealousy is not the petty thing the word suggests in human relationships. It is the proper response of a husband to a wife who is leaving — and a God who felt nothing about our adultery would not be more loving but less. Indifference is not the opposite of jealousy; it is the opposite of love.

Then verse 6, and after the severity of verses 1–5 it arrives like a door opening: “But he gives more grace.”

Four words, and they are the turning point of the chapter and arguably of the letter. More grace — greater than the adultery, greater than the quarrelling, greater than the appetite that has been running the whole congregation. Whatever the sin has cost, the supply is larger.

“Therefore it says, ‘God opposes the proud but gives grace to the humble.’” The quotation is Proverbs 3:34, and Peter uses it too (1 Pet 5:5) — evidently a text the early church leaned on.

And it names the one condition. Grace is not scarce; it is more. But it is given downhill, and it will not flow to a man who has arranged himself above it. The word for opposes is military — to set oneself in array against. God does not merely withhold from the proud. He lines up against them.

verseByVerse.quote: Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you. Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now ten imperatives in four verses — the densest cluster of commands in the letter. And they all unpack the single word at the end of verse 6: the humble.

“Submit yourselves therefore to God.” A military word again — to arrange yourself under. It is the opposite of the proud man’s posture, and it is first because everything else follows from it.

“Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” Note the order: submit first, then resist. A man who has not submitted to God has no standing from which to resist anything. And the promise is remarkable — not that the devil will be defeated after a long struggle, but that he will flee. He does not have the resources for a siege.

“Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you.” The language is priestly — it is what a priest did when he approached the altar. James applies to ordinary believers the vocabulary of the sanctuary.

And the promise should be read carefully. It is not that God waits at a distance until we have travelled far enough. The whole chapter has just said he yearns jealously over us and gives more grace. The drawing near is a response to a God who is already leaning toward us — and the prodigal’s father, who ran, is the right picture.

Then two commands with two vocatives, and they are addressed to church members: “Cleanse your hands, you sinners, and purify your hearts, you double-minded.”

Hands and hearts — outward conduct and inward loyalty, and both are required. And there is dipsychos again, the two-souled word James coined in 1:8. It is his diagnosis for the whole letter, and here at last it is given a remedy: not effort, but purification — and it comes after “he gives more grace.”

verseByVerse.quote: Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom. Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Be wretched and mourn and weep. Let your laughter be turned to mourning and your joy to gloom.”

It is the most severe thing in the letter, and it sits oddly in a New Testament that commands rejoicing — James himself opened by telling them to count trials all joy. So what is going on?

The answer is that this is a call to repentance, and repentance has an appropriate emotional weather. James is addressing people who have been quarrelling, coveting and committing spiritual adultery — and doing it cheerfully. The laughter he wants turned to mourning is the laughter of people who are not taking their condition seriously.

This is not a call to permanent gloom, and it is not a recommendation of misery as a spiritual state. It is the recognition that there is a grief which is the right response to your own sin, and that a person who can survey what James has just described without any of it has not understood. Paul calls it godly grief, and says it produces a repentance without regret (2 Cor 7:10).

“Humble yourselves before the Lord, and he will exalt you.” The tenth imperative, and it closes the sequence by returning to the proverb of verse 6.

Note who does the humbling and who does the exalting. The humbling is commanded — it is ours, and it is active. The exalting is promised, and it is his. That order is the whole of biblical spirituality, and it is the exact reverse of the arrangement everyone defaults to, in which we exalt ourselves and hope God will not humble us.

And it is a promise, not merely a condition. The man who goes low is not left there. James does not say humility is its own reward; he says God lifts the person who takes the low place — which is the pattern of Christ himself (Phil 2:8–9), though James does not say so.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Do not speak against one another; the one who judges a brother judges the law, and a judge of the law is not a doer of it (v.11). There is one lawgiver and judge, able to save and destroy — who are you to judge your neighbour (v.12)?

Come now, you who say you will go to such a town, spend a year, trade and make a profit (v.13) — yet you do not know what tomorrow brings, and you are a mist that appears briefly and vanishes (v.14). You ought rather to say, if the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that (v.15). As it is you boast in your arrogance, and all such boasting is evil (v.16). So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin (v.17).
verseByVerse.theology:
Sin as Knowledge Not Acted On

Verse 17 reads like a detached proverb and is not; the “so” ties it to the business plan. These men now know about the mist and the “if the Lord wills”, and from this point their planning cannot be excused as thoughtlessness. James closes the exit.

And the definition of sin here is not the usual one. Sin is normally defined as doing what is forbidden; James defines it as not doing what is known to be right — omission, and specifically knowledge that has not been acted on. Which is the whole letter compressed: the man who hears and does not do deceives himself (1:22), the man who says and does not give is useless (2:16), the man who knows and does not act is sinning. James’s charge is never that his readers are ignorant. It is that they are informed — a sobering thought for anyone who reads much and has a shelf of books, since the liability grows with every sermon understood.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Verse 11’s argument is shrewd. Criticising a person becomes criticising the law because the law says love your neighbour as yourself (2:8); set that aside to condemn somebody and you have not merely disobeyed it but passed judgement on it, ruling that here it does not apply. Chapter 1 divided the world into hearers and doers; here it is doers and judges, and you cannot be both, because a judge stands over the law and a doer stands under it.

Now: Notice how complete the business plan of verse 13 is — timing, destination, duration, activity and outcome, all settled — and that nothing in it is condemned. Trade is not condemned, profit is not, planning is not. What is missing is one clause, and the correction in verse 15 is smaller than we expect: not cancel the trip, but add “if the Lord wills” — which covers not only the doing but the living. It is not a formula to attach to sentences; a man can say the words with no such acknowledgement, and another can plan his whole year in that spirit without saying them once.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not speak evil against one another, brothers. The one who speaks against a brother or judges his brother, speaks evil against the law and judges the law. But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge. There is only one lawgiver and judge, he who is able to save and to destroy. But who are you to judge your neighbor?
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not speak evil against one another, brothers.” The word means to talk down, to speak against — and it covers the whole range from slander to the accurate but damaging remark. It is the tongue of chapter 3 turned on the congregation.

Then an argument that is easy to miss and is remarkably shrewd: “The one who speaks against a brother or judges his brother, speaks against the law and judges the law.”

How does criticising a person become criticising the law? Because the law says love your neighbour as yourself — the royal law of 2:8. If you set that aside in order to condemn somebody, you have not merely disobeyed it. You have passed judgement on it, ruling that in this case it does not apply.

“But if you judge the law, you are not a doer of the law but a judge.” And there is the whole letter’s theme again, in a new setting. Chapter 1 divided the world into hearers and doers; here it is doers and judges. You cannot be both, because a judge stands over the law and a doer stands under it.

“There is only one lawgiver and judge, he who is able to save and to destroy.” The credentials are decisive. The one qualified to judge is the one who can act on the verdict either way, and that describes exactly one person.

“But who are you to judge your neighbour?” The question is not rhetorical bluster; it is a genuine matter of jurisdiction. And note the last word — neighbour, which pulls Leviticus 19:18 back into the sentence one final time. The person you are judging is the person you were commanded to love.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you who say, “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit”— yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring. What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes. Instead you ought to say, “If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.”
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Come now, you who say…” It is the prophet’s summons — a phrase for calling someone to account, and James will use it again at 5:1.

Then he quotes the business plan, and it is entirely reasonable: “Today or tomorrow we will go into such and such a town and spend a year there and trade and make a profit.”

Look at how complete it is. The timing, the destination, the duration, the activity and the outcome — five elements, all settled. And there is nothing wrong with any of them. Trade is not condemned here, profit is not condemned, and planning is not condemned; Scripture commends the ant who prepares in summer.

What is missing is one word, and James supplies it in verse 15.

“Yet you do not know what tomorrow will bring.” That is not pessimism, it is arithmetic. The plan assumes access to information nobody has.

“What is your life? For you are a mist that appears for a little time and then vanishes.” The word is used of steam or morning haze — the vapour over a field that is gone once the sun is properly up. Not a short life. A brief appearance.

“Instead you ought to say, ‘If the Lord wills, we will live and do this or that.’” And the correction is smaller than we expect. James does not tell them to cancel the trip or abandon the trade. He tells them to add a clause — and the clause covers not only the doing but the living: if the Lord wills, we will live, and then we will do.

This is not a formula to be attached to sentences. It is an acknowledgement to be held in the mind, and a man can say the words with no such acknowledgement while another plans his whole year in that spirit without saying them once.

verseByVerse.quote: As it is, you boast in your arrogance. All such boasting is evil. So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“As it is, you boast in your arrogance.” The word for arrogance originally described the wandering quack — the travelling impostor who claimed powers he did not have. It is exactly right for a man announcing what next year holds.

“All such boasting is evil.” Not unwise, not naive. Evil — because it is a claim to a knowledge and a control that belong to God alone, made by a mist.

Then verse 17, which reads like a detached proverb and is not: “So whoever knows the right thing to do and fails to do it, for him it is sin.”

The “so” ties it to what precedes. These men now know about the mist and the “if the Lord wills.” They have been told. From this point their planning cannot be excused as thoughtlessness, and James closes the exit.

And the definition of sin here is worth weighing, because it is not the usual one. Sin is normally defined as doing what is forbidden. James defines it as not doing what is known to be right — sin as omission, and specifically as knowledge that has not been acted on.

Which is the whole letter compressed into a sentence. The man who hears and does not do is deceiving himself (1:22); the man who says and does not give is useless (2:16); the man who knows and does not act is sinning. James’s consistent charge is never that his readers are ignorant. It is that they are informed.

And that is a sobering thought for anyone who reads much, hears much, and has a shelf of books. The verse creates a liability that grows with every sermon understood and every chapter agreed with. Knowing more is not a neutral achievement.

5.title: Patient Until He Comes: Wealth, Endurance, and Prayer
5.overview:
The final chapter of James brings together the letter’s major themes in a conclusion that moves from prophetic warning to pastoral tenderness. The opening passage (vv. 1–6) is the most severe in the letter: a woe oracle against the wealthy who have oppressed the poor, withheld wages, and lived in luxury while the righteous suffer. This is not a general warning about the spiritual dangers of wealth; it is a specific indictment of wealthy oppressors who have used their power against the most vulnerable, and whose judgment is certain.

Against this dark background, the letter turns to the suffering community with pastoral warmth. The patience of the farmer who waits for the rains (vv. 7–11) is the model: you cannot hurry the harvest; you can only wait, watching for the rains, knowing that the harvest is coming. The coming of the Lord is the horizon that makes patience possible — not resignation to injustice but confidence that the Judge is at the door and that he will make all things right. The examples of the prophets and of Job encourage: those who endured affliction under the old covenant discovered the compassion and mercy of the Lord on the other side.

The letter ends where the Christian life begins and always returns: prayer. The effectual prayer of a righteous person has great power (v. 16). Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and his prayer shut and opened the rain. The community of prayer is the community that is simultaneously most realistic about its need (confessing sins to one another) and most confident about its resource (the God who hears and acts). And the final word of the letter is not about doctrine or practice but about people: if any one among you wanders, and someone brings them back, they have covered a multitude of sins. The community that prays together is the community that reaches for the wanderer — and that reaching is, James says, one of the greatest works of grace.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries coming on you (v.1). Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten (v.2); your gold and silver have corroded, and the corrosion is evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire — you have laid up treasure in the last days (v.3).

Behold, the wages of the labourers who mowed your fields, kept back by fraud, are crying out, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts (v.4). You have lived in luxury and self-indulgence, fattening your hearts in a day of slaughter (v.5). You have condemned and murdered the righteous person, and he does not resist you (v.6).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Rust That Testifies

James lists three assets in ascending order of durability, and all three have failed — and the third is chemically impossible. Gold does not corrode; that is precisely why it has been money for five thousand years. The overstatement is the point: the one asset that cannot decay has.

And the corrosion is called evidence, a legal term for testimony for the prosecution. What it testifies to is that the wealth sat unused — metal that is spent does not corrode. This corroded because it was hoarded while the men who earned it went hungry. Then the final irony: they were accumulating “in the last days”, like a man buying property in a town he knows is to be flooded. The folly is not the wealth; it is the timing.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: The charge in verse 4 is specific and the law was explicit about it. A hired man was to be paid the same day, before sunset, because he is poor and counting on it (Lev 19:13; Deut 24:14–15). A day-labourer had no savings; the wage bought that evening’s food, so withholding it overnight was not a cashflow decision but a family going without supper. The verb for their crying is the one used of Abel’s blood crying from the ground (Gen 4:10), and “Lord of hosts” is the military title. Men with no advocate, no court and no standing have had their case heard by the commander of heaven’s armies.

Now: Note that James is not condemning wealth in the abstract but a specific transfer — comfort at one table bought by hunger at another. And “you have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter” is a terrible image: the beast grazes contentedly and does not know what the day is for. They took their prosperity as evidence of favour; James says it was fattening. The last sentence is the most terrible of all — “he does not resist you.” There was never a contest.

verseByVerse.quote: Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted and your garments are moth-eaten. Your gold and silver have corroded, and their corrosion will be evidence against you and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up treasure in the last days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Come now, you rich, weep and howl.” The verb is violent — to shriek, the noise of open grief. This is prophetic denunciation in the manner of Amos, and it is worth noting that James is almost certainly not addressing members of the congregation here. He addresses the oppressors directly, as the prophets did, while the oppressed listen.

“For the miseries that are coming upon you.” Not that have come. The judgement is future and certain, and the weeping is commanded now on account of it.

Then three assets, in ascending order of durability, and all three have failed. “Your riches have rotted” — the general word, and rot is what happens to grain and produce. “Your garments are moth-eaten” — fine clothing was stored wealth in that world, and a moth needs no thief. “Your gold and silver have corroded.”

That third one is chemically impossible, and James knows it. Gold does not corrode; that is precisely why it has been money for five thousand years. He is making a point by overstatement: the one asset that cannot decay has decayed. Nothing they own has survived.

“And their corrosion will be evidence against you.” The word is a legal term — testimony for the prosecution. The rust is a witness, and what it testifies to is that the wealth sat unused. Metal that is spent does not corrode. This corroded because it was hoarded while the men who earned it went hungry.

“And will eat your flesh like fire.” The image turns on them bodily: the corrosion that consumed the treasure will consume the owner.

“You have laid up treasure in the last days.” That is the final irony. They were accumulating in the very period when it could least be of use — like a man buying property in a town he knows is to be flooded. The folly is not the wealth. It is the timing.

verseByVerse.quote: Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts. You have lived on the earth in luxury and in self-indulgence. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter. You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. He does not resist you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Now the specific charge, and it is not vague: “the wages of the labourers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud.”

The Old Testament is explicit about this. A hired man was to be paid the same day, before sunset, because he is poor and counting on it (Lev 19:13; Deut 24:14–15). A day-labourer had no savings; the wage bought that evening’s food. To withhold it overnight was not a cashflow decision. It was a family going without supper.

“Are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts.” Two cries: the wages themselves cry, and so do the men. The verb is the one used of Abel’s blood crying from the ground (Gen 4:10), and “Lord of hosts” is the military title — the LORD of armies. James chooses it deliberately. The defrauded workers have no advocate, no court and no standing. Their case has been heard by the commander of heaven’s armies.

“You have lived on the earth in luxury and self-indulgence.” The two words are soft living and wanton pleasure, and the contrast is the whole point — this luxury was funded by that unpaid wage. James is not condemning wealth in the abstract but a specific transfer: comfort at one table bought by hunger at another.

“You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter.” A terrible image. The beast is grazing contentedly, and it does not know what the day is for. They took their prosperity as evidence of favour; James says it was fattening.

“You have condemned and murdered the righteous person. He does not resist you.” Condemned is a courtroom word — the machinery of law used against a man who could not afford it (cf. 2:6). And the last sentence is the most terrible: he is not resisting. There was never a contest.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–20 — Patience, Prayer, and Going After the Wanderer
verseByVerse.sectionOverview:
Be patient until the coming of the Lord, as the farmer waits for the early and late rains (v.7); establish your hearts, for his coming is at hand (v.8). Do not grumble against one another — the Judge is standing at the door (v.9). Take the prophets as an example of suffering and patience (v.10); we call those blessed who remained steadfast, and you have heard of Job and seen the Lord’s purpose, how he is compassionate and merciful (v.11). Above all, do not swear, but let your yes be yes and your no be no (v.12).

Suffering? Pray. Cheerful? Sing praise (v.13). Sick? Call the elders to pray over him and anoint him with oil (v.14); the prayer of faith will save him and the Lord will raise him up, and if he has sinned he will be forgiven (v.15). So confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, for a righteous person’s prayer has great power in its working (v.16) — Elijah, a man of like nature with us, prayed and it did not rain for three and a half years (v.17), and prayed again and the heavens gave rain (v.18).

Finally: if anyone wanders from the truth and someone brings him back (v.19), let him know that whoever turns a sinner from his wandering will save a soul from death and cover a multitude of sins (v.20).
verseByVerse.theology:
The Prayer of Faith, Handled Honestly

Verse 15 read flatly promises that every believing prayer heals, and every Christian knows it does not. Several things keep it from meaning that. The letter has just said asking can be answered no when the asking is wrong (4:3). Paul prayed three times about his thorn and was refused (2 Cor 12:8–9), and left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Tim 4:20). And “the prayer of faith” is not prayer accompanied by sufficient confidence — faith of that kind would be a work, and its absence would make a sick man’s illness his own fault, which is precisely the cruelty this verse has been used to inflict.

Better to read it as prayer offered in submission to God’s will, which is what faith always is in this letter. The verbs support it: “save” and “raise up” both reach further than physical recovery, and the final raising is guaranteed to every believer whether or not this illness ends. Note too the careful conditional — “if he has committed sins” — which allows that sin may be involved and refuses to assume it. That is exactly the balance Job’s friends failed to keep.
verseByVerse.examples:
Then: Job repays thought as an example, because he was not patient in the sense the English phrase has acquired. He protested at length, demanded an audience and told God he had a case to argue. What he did was not let go, which is what hypomone means — so James’s steadfastness plainly has room for a man who complains bitterly and will not walk away. And note that the Lord is called “compassionate and merciful” on the strength of a book that contains no explanation of the suffering at all. James does not say God explained himself; he says the end of the story showed what he was like.

Now: Verse 9’s placing is shrewd. Told to be patient with oppressors they cannot answer, the pressure goes sideways — onto the people nearest. A congregation strained from outside turns on itself, and the form is rarely dramatic; it is muttering. And “the Judge is standing at the door” does two things at once: it comforts the oppressed of verses 1–6, whose Judge has arrived at the building, and it warns the same people in the same breath, since he is at the door of their room too. Note finally how the letter ends — no benediction, no greetings, no signature. Just the most concrete act of love available to an ordinary Christian: noticing that someone has stopped coming, and going to find out why.

verseByVerse.quote: Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient about it, until it receives the early and the late rains. You also, be patient. Establish your hearts, for the coming of the Lord is at hand.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Be patient, therefore, brothers.” The address changes back to the congregation, and everything softens. The word is not the hypomone of chapter 1, which is endurance under weight. It is makrothymia — long-tempered, slow to burn, the patience shown toward difficult people.

Which is exactly right after verses 1–6. Having heard their oppressors denounced, the natural next move is to take matters up themselves. James says: wait.

“Until the coming of the Lord.” And that is the ground of it. He is not telling them the injustice does not matter or that it will resolve itself. He has just said the Lord of hosts has heard. The waiting is not for nothing to happen; it is for someone else to act.

“See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth… until it receives the early and the late rains.” The picture is precisely local. Palestinian agriculture depends on autumn rains to soften the ground for sowing and spring rains to swell the grain before harvest, and between them lie months in which nothing can be done.

The farmer’s patience is not passivity — he has ploughed and sown, and he will reap. But there is a stretch in the middle where all the activity in the world would not bring the harvest forward by a day, and the mark of a farmer is that he knows it.

“Establish your hearts” — the word means to make firm, to prop. Waiting is not merely refraining; it requires something to be shored up.

“For the coming of the Lord is at hand.” Not far off. That is the whole reason the waiting is bearable, and say it plainly plainly that James expected it soon. The New Testament’s consistent posture is imminence — not a date, but a nearness that makes patience reasonable rather than resigned.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not grumble against one another, brothers, so that you may not be judged; behold, the Judge is standing at the door.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Do not grumble against one another, brothers.” The word means to groan or sigh — and it is not the sound of open quarrelling but of muttering. The complaint under the breath, the remark to one person about another.

The placing is shrewd. James has just told them to be patient toward their oppressors — and he knows exactly where that pressure goes. Pressure from outside that cannot be discharged outward is discharged sideways, onto the people nearest. A congregation under strain from without turns on itself, and the form it takes is rarely dramatic. It is grumbling.

“So that you may not be judged.” The warning connects directly to 4:11–12, where judging a brother usurped the one Lawgiver’s office. To grumble is to pass sentence privately, and the man who convenes his own court will find himself in somebody else’s.

“Behold, the Judge is standing at the door.” It is one of the most vivid sentences in the letter, and it does two things at once.

It is a comfort. The oppressed of verses 1–6 are told their Judge has not merely heard the case — he has arrived at the building.

And it is a warning to the same people in the same breath. He is at the door of their room too, and he is about to walk in on the muttering. James gives them no opportunity to enjoy the judgement of their enemies without noticing where they are standing themselves.

verseByVerse.quote: As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord. Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast. You have heard of the steadfastness of Job, and you have seen the purpose of the Lord, how the Lord is compassionate and merciful.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“As an example of suffering and patience, brothers, take the prophets who spoke in the name of the Lord.”

The choice is pointed. The prophets were not men who suffered despite their faithfulness; they suffered because of it, and specifically because they spoke in the Lord’s name. James is telling a congregation being oppressed for their faith that they are in the succession, not the exception.

“Behold, we consider those blessed who remained steadfast.” And here the word returns to hypomone, the endurance of chapter 1 — and to “blessed”, which picks up 1:12 exactly. The letter is closing its own circle.

“You have heard of the steadfastness of Job.” The example repays thought, because Job was not patient in the sense the phrase has acquired in English. He protested at length, demanded an audience, and told God he had a case to argue. What he did was not let go — which is what hypomone means. James’s idea of steadfastness plainly has room for a man who complains bitterly and will not walk away.

“And you have seen the purpose of the Lord.” The phrase means the end, the outcome — how it turned out. Job could not see it from inside; the reader of the book can, and that is the advantage James is handing them.

“How the Lord is compassionate and merciful.” That is a remarkable conclusion to draw from the book of Job, which contains no explanation of his suffering at all. James does not say the Lord explained himself. He says the end of the story showed what he was like — and the two words he chooses are the ancient self-description of God at Sinai (Exod 34:6).

verseByVerse.quote: But above all, my brothers, do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath, but let your “yes” be yes and your “no” be no, so that you may not fall under condemnation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“But above all, my brothers, do not swear.” The phrase is arresting. Above all what? Not the whole letter — James can hardly mean this matters more than faith and works. It is most likely a way of flagging a final point of importance, and it echoes his brother almost word for word (Matt 5:34–37).

The oath-taking in view is not courtroom testimony, and it is not blasphemy. It is the habit of reinforcing your own speech: swearing by heaven, by earth, by the temple, by your own head — a graded system in which some oaths were held binding and others were understood to be escape routes.

That is what makes it a speech problem rather than a religious one, and it belongs to a letter that has said so much about the tongue. A man who must swear to be believed has admitted that his ordinary word is not reliable.

“But let your ‘yes’ be yes and your ‘no’ be no.” The remedy is not more solemn language but less. If a man’s plain word holds, he needs no machinery to prop it up — and the machinery is itself evidence that something is wrong.

“So that you may not fall under condemnation.” The stakes are higher than the subject seems to warrant, and that is the point. A graded oath system is a device for deceiving while appearing truthful, and God is not deceived by the gradations.

The practical question this puts is small and searching. Do the people who know you best need you to insist? A person whose word is simply good has no use for emphasis, and the habit of over-assurance is usually a sign that somewhere the plain word has stopped being enough.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray. Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three questions in quick succession, each with a one-word answer, and together they map the whole emotional range of a Christian life onto prayer and praise.

“Is anyone among you suffering? Let him pray.” The word covers hardship generally — the same root as the “suffering” of the prophets in verse 10. And the response is not resignation, not stoicism, and not a search for the reason. Pray.

“Is anyone cheerful? Let him sing praise.” And that is the half we habitually neglect. Most Christians know that trouble should send them to God; far fewer treat gladness as equally directional.

The pairing is the point. There is no condition in which the answer is to do nothing God-ward. Trouble goes up as prayer, joy goes up as song, and between them they cover every day anybody has.

It is also a quiet correction of a besetting error, which is to treat God as an emergency service. A man who prays only when suffering has a relationship with his own need rather than with God — and the second question is there to expose it.

And note that James does not require the cheerful man to become solemn before he approaches. The gladness itself is what goes up. This is the same writer who told them to count trials joy and to let laughter turn to mourning when repenting — he is not against any emotion. He is against every emotion being kept to oneself.

verseByVerse.quote: Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the church.” Note who initiates: the sick man calls. And note the plural — not the gifted individual but the elders, the ordinary appointed leadership of the local congregation.

“And let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.” The main verb is pray; the anointing is a participle, subordinate to it. Oil in that world was both medicine (the Samaritan poured oil on the wounds) and a sign of consecration. Whether the gesture here is chiefly medical or symbolic, it is not the operative thing — the praying is, and it is done “in the name of the Lord.”

“And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up.”

This has to be handled honestly, because read flatly it promises that every believing prayer heals, and every Christian knows it does not. Several things keep it from meaning that. The letter itself has just said that asking can be answered no when the asking is wrong (4:3). Paul prayed three times about his thorn and was refused (2 Cor 12:8–9), and left Trophimus ill at Miletus (2 Tim 4:20). And “the prayer of faith” is not prayer accompanied by sufficient confidence — faith of that kind would be a work, and its absence would make the sick man’s illness his own fault, which is precisely the cruelty this verse has often been used to inflict.

Better to take it as prayer offered in submission to God’s will, which is what faith always is in this letter — and the verbs support it. “Save” and “raise up” are both words with a larger reach than physical recovery, and the final raising up is guaranteed for every believer whether or not this illness ends.

“And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven.” The conditional is careful and merciful. James allows that sin may be involved and refuses to assume it — which is exactly the balance Job’s friends failed to keep.

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Therefore, confess your sins to one another and pray for one another, that you may be healed.”

The “therefore” follows the conditional clause about sin. Since sin may sometimes lie behind trouble, deal with it — and deal with it in the open.

Note the direction: to one another. Not to a priest, and not to God only. James is describing something mutual and horizontal — ordinary Christians telling each other the truth about themselves. It requires no office and it is available in any congregation, and it is almost universally avoided.

The reason it is avoided is the reason it works. Sin kept private grows in the dark and is fed by the fear of exposure; the man who has told somebody has already lost the thing that was protecting it. And the pairing matters — confession alone leaves a person exposed, so James joins it to intercession. You tell someone, and they pray for you.

“The prayer of a righteous person has great power as it is working.” The last phrase is difficult and probably means in its working — that is, prayer is not a stored potency but something powerful in operation, effective as it is being prayed.

And “righteous” should not be read as a rare spiritual class, or the whole verse becomes a discouragement to the very people it is written for. The next verse settles it decisively: the righteous man James has in mind is Elijah, and the first thing he says about him is that he was made of exactly the same stuff we are.

verseByVerse.quote: Elijah was a man with a nature like ours, and he prayed fervently that it might not rain, and for three years and six months it did not rain on the earth. Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.
verseByVerse.commentary:
“Elijah was a man with a nature like ours.” James puts that first, before anything about the miracle, and it is the whole reason he chose the example.

Elijah is the most spectacular figure in the prophetic history — fire from heaven on Carmel, the ravens, the chariot. He is exactly the man a discouraged congregation would cite as proof that prayer works for other people. So James disarms the objection in the first clause: same nature, same stuff.

And the account bears him out. This is the prophet who, immediately after the greatest answered prayer in the Old Testament, ran into the desert and asked God to let him die (1 Kgs 19:4). Whatever Elijah was, he was not temperamentally immune to despair.

“And he prayed fervently that it might not rain.” The Greek is a Hebrew idiom — literally he prayed with prayer — which conveys earnestness. and notice that 1 Kings does not actually record him praying for the drought; it records him announcing it. James, or the tradition he knows, understands the announcement to have rested on prayer — which says something about where a prophet’s public word comes from.

“And for three years and six months it did not rain.” The Lord gives the same figure (Luke 4:25).

“Then he prayed again, and heaven gave rain, and the earth bore its fruit.” Both directions — the withholding and the giving — came through the same channel. And the closing image is agricultural, which returns to the farmer of verse 7 waiting for the early and late rains. The letter’s pictures are tying themselves together as it ends.

verseByVerse.quote: My brothers, if anyone among you wanders from the truth and someone brings him back, let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death and will cover a multitude of sins.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The letter ends without a benediction, without greetings, without a signature. It simply stops — on the subject of somebody else’s soul.

“If anyone among you wanders from the truth.” The verb is to be led astray, to go off course — the same root as our “planet”, the wandering star. It is drift, not a decision. Nobody announces that they are leaving.

“And someone brings him back.” Note how ordinary that someone is. Not the elders of verse 14, not a teacher, not an office. Someone — anyone who notices and goes after him.

“Let him know that whoever brings back a sinner from his wandering will save his soul from death.” That is as high a claim as could be made for a piece of personal pastoral work, and it is made about an unnamed church member.

“And will cover a multitude of sins” — an echo of Proverbs 10:12. The covering is God’s work; the human agent is the occasion of it, not the cause. Whose sins are covered is left slightly open, and probably deliberately: the man restored is forgiven, and the one who went after him has been doing the very thing this whole letter has demanded, which is to be a doer.

And that is a fitting last word. James has spent five chapters insisting that faith shows, that hearing is not doing, that religion is visited widows and unstained lives, and that the tongue reveals the heart. He ends by describing the most concrete act of love available to an ordinary Christian: noticing that someone has stopped coming, and going to find out why.

No farewell. Just a man walking out to look for somebody.
